title: The page builder tax: what drag-and-drop really costs
excerpt: Drag-and-drop is cheap to start and expensive to keep. Where the cost shows up, and what the alternative actually looks like.
answerBlock: A page builder saves money once and charges it back every month, in page weight, in editing time and in content you cannot easily take elsewhere. The cost compounds because every section ships its own styles and scripts, so the site gets heavier with each page somebody adds. The alternative is not hand-coding: it is a small set of database-backed content types with their own editors.

seo.title: What a page builder really costs you
seo.description: Where a page builder charges you back: page weight, editing time and content you cannot export. And what the alternative looks like.

author.name: Priya Raman
author.bio: Runs the design system and every high-fidelity screen you approve.

takeaways: A page builder trades a small, visible saving at the start for an invisible cost paid every month afterwards, in speed, in editing time and in the freedom to leave.
The tax compounds because every section carries its own styles and scripts, so a site gets heavier with each page somebody adds.
Builder markup is proprietary. Your content leaves as shortcodes and nested containers rather than as text, which is what makes migration expensive.
The alternative is not hand-coding every page. It is a small set of database-backed content types with their own editors, which is faster to publish with, not slower.
If you are already on one, fix the templates that earn money first. A full rebuild is rarely the right first move.
body:
## What is the page builder tax?

It is the difference between what a drag-and-drop site costs to start and what it costs to keep. The first number is small and visible; the second is large and arrives in instalments, which is why so few companies notice they are paying it.

It shows up as pages that take five seconds to load on a phone. As a marketing team that needs a developer anyway, because the layout breaks whenever the copy is longer than the mock-up. As a section that cannot be reused, so the same content is pasted into nine pages and updated in one. And, eventually, as a quote to rebuild that is larger than the original project, because the content has to be extracted from the builder before it can go anywhere else.

None of this is an argument against visual editing. It is an argument against a particular kind of visual editing, where layout and content are stored together in a format only that tool understands.

## Where does the cost actually show up?

In four places, roughly in this order.

| Where | What it looks like | Who pays |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Each section loads its own styles and scripts | Every visitor, on every page |
| Editing | Layout breaks when copy grows, so edits need care | Your marketing team, weekly |
| Consistency | Nine versions of the same section, none identical | Your brand, quietly |
| Exit | Content stored as builder markup, not as content | You, once, expensively |

The last row is the one that decides how trapped you are. Everything else is a performance problem you can attack incrementally.

## Why does a builder site get slower over time?

Because the architecture rewards addition and never punishes it.

A page builder cannot know which of its hundred section types you will use, so it ships the machinery for all of the ones on the page, plus a general layer to arrange them. Add a slider, a counter, a tabbed block and an animated icon set, and you have four libraries, each of which was fine on its own.

The visible symptom is a Largest Contentful Paint that drifts past the 2.5 second threshold Google publishes for a good score ([Core Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)). The underlying cause is usually a mix of unoptimised images and third-party scripts, which is well documented as one of the most common brakes on a page ([third-party JavaScript](https://web.dev/articles/third-party-javascript)). The long-term trend in page weight is public, and it goes in one direction; the HTTP Archive tracks it month by month ([page weight report](https://httparchive.org/reports/page-weight)).

What makes builders particular is that the growth is invisible to the person causing it. Nobody adds a section thinking they have made the site slower. They have.

## What happens to your content when you leave?

This is the part worth understanding before you start, not after.

In a well-structured site, a service page is a record: a title, an answer, a list of deliverables, some frequently asked questions, an image and its alt text. Those fields can be exported, reimported, rendered differently, or handed to a different agency, because they are content.

In a builder, the same page is stored as nested containers with styling attributes, wrapped around fragments of text. Export it and you get markup. Somebody then has to open every page and copy the words out by hand, which is exactly the migration cost that keeps companies on tools they have outgrown. WordPress's own block editor stores structured blocks in the post content, which is considerably better than shortcode-based builders, but the principle still applies: the more layout you bake into the content, the less portable the content is ([block editor documentation](https://developer.wordpress.org/block-editor/)).

Verona Home is a recognisable version of this. A furniture brand whose catalogue had outgrown a builder that could not model made-to-order pieces, so every configuration option lived in a paragraph rather than in a field. The [replatform](/work/verona-home/) was as much a data exercise as a design one.

## Is a page builder ever the right answer?

Yes, and it is worth saying plainly.

For a brochure site of eight pages that will not change much, for a campaign microsite with a three-month life, or for a company with no budget and no developer, a builder is a sensible, honest choice. The tax is small when the site is small and short-lived.

It stops being the right answer at the point where the site becomes an operational asset: when the same page shape repeats dozens of times, when publishing is somebody's actual job, when the site has to talk to another system, or when organic search is a meaningful channel. At that point the builder stops saving time and starts spending it.

## What does the alternative look like?

Not a site where every page needs a developer. That is the false choice builders are sold against, and it is worth dismantling.

The alternative is a handful of content types with their own editors. A service is a record with defined fields. A case study is a record. A location page is a record. Each has one template, designed once, and the person publishing fills in fields rather than arranging boxes. Publishing a new service page takes ten minutes and cannot break the layout, because there is no layout to break.

The trade is honest: you give up arbitrary per-page arrangement, and you get speed, consistency and content you own. For a company with fifty service pages that should all look alike, that is not a sacrifice; it is the point. That is what a [custom build with real content types](/services/custom-website-development/) means in practice, and it is why our own platform has no page builder in it.

## How do you move off one without losing rankings?

Carefully, and in this order.

Inventory first. Export every URL with its traffic and its conversions, and mark the pages that actually earn. On most sites it is a small fraction, and that fraction decides the plan.

Extract the content as content. Go through the earning pages and pull the words into fields: title, answer, body, list items, questions and answers. This is manual and it is the real cost of leaving. Do it once, properly, and it never has to happen again.

Rebuild the templates, not the pages. Ten templates usually cover a hundred pages. Then the content you extracted flows into them.

Map every URL before launch, with a permanent redirect for anything that moves, because a 301 is the signal that transfers the page's history to its new address ([Google on redirects](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/301-redirects)).

If a full move is not affordable this year, the pragmatic version is to rebuild only the templates that earn and leave the rest where they are. A [staged redesign](/services/website-redesign/) is less satisfying than a clean break, and it is usually the right call commercially.

## What should you ask before committing to a builder?

Four questions, and the answers take five minutes to find.

How does content come out, and in what format? Ask for an export of one page and look at it.

What does a page weigh, and how much of that is the builder itself? Load a demo site on a phone over mobile data, not on your laptop.

Who can change a template, and what happens when a section needs to appear on forty pages at once?

And what does year three look like, when there are two hundred pages, three people editing and nobody left who remembers how the first ten were built? That is the question the tax is really about.
